name: Leech the weapon of what you destroy
summary: A unit turns enemy losses into its own power. It first claims a donor: a tether held on the target, a finishing blow, or touching the wreck or a dropped item. When the donor dies, something moves to the claimer: a copy of the donor's weapon (so the reward depends on what was killed), a generic upgrade step, the donor's whole vehicle, or materials. The usual limits are one slot or a short ladder of upgrades, a short window to claim, and a vulnerable claiming state. It changes what a kill means: players pick targets by what they will get, and damaged players learn to back off before they become loot.
counterplay: Break the claim: leave tether range or break line of sight before you die, so the enemy gets nothing.
Attack the claimer while it is busy: claiming usually silences its main gun and slows or roots it.
Deny the leftovers: destroy wrecks, crates and dropped weapons, or reach them first.
Bring units that give nothing useful, or nothing that fills the claimer's gap (for example no anti-air donors).
Use aircraft against ground claimers that can't tether them.
Use hard counters against the stolen weapon itself, such as point defence against salvaged rockets.

other_examples.unit: Salvage crates (GLA Technical, Marauder, Scorpion and others)
other_examples.note: Destroyed vehicles drop crates that only the leeching faction can see. Each compatible vehicle climbs a fixed two-step upgrade ladder, whatever the donor was; vehicles already at the top get a little cash and experience instead.
The whole-vehicle version: an unarmed, stealthy soldier takes most enemy vehicles on contact and keeps their veterancy, and climbs out to steal another when the vehicle dies.
A one-at-a-time commando that can steal any vehicle, even the heaviest walkers, and pops out to steal again when it is destroyed.

other_examples.game: extra:Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars / Kane's Wrath
other_examples.unit: Avatar walker's commandeer, and walker husks (Nod)
other_examples.note: The Avatar rips modules off other vehicles, friendly ones included, destroying them, and mounts them on itself (a flamethrower, a cloak, a second beam). Heavy walkers leave husks that an engineer from either side can revive.

other_examples.unit: Dropped weapons and abandoned team weapons (all factions)
other_examples.note: Specialist weapons drop when their carrier dies and any squad can pick them up, enemies included; crew-served guns left without a crew can be manned by anyone.

shooter_analogues.note: A pilot rips the battery out of an enemy Titan, which damages it, and carries it to a friendly Titan for a shield and health boost; the carrier drops it on death, so the enemy can chase it back.
A killed player's kit can be picked up and used at once; dropped kits vanish after a short time.
Beating a boss permanently gives its weapon, which runs on limited energy that must be refilled: the cleanest 'kill it, get its gun' with an ammo limit.

sources.title: Special Weapon, Mega Man Knowledge Base

shooter_analogues.note: Destroyed machines drop power cells that recharge shields mid-fight and parts that become crafting material: kills pay out in resources rather than guns.
Throwing a driver out and taking the seat: the whole-vehicle version in a shooter.

player_translation.summary: A mid-tier vehicle with a main gun and a long-reach tether. Hold the tether on a target the team is killing; if it dies while tethered, whoever landed the kill, a copy of its weapon snaps onto your chassis.
as_user: The choice is tether or shoot: while tethered your main gun is silent and you are slowed or rooted. Good players tether the target their team is already focusing.
Target choice becomes a shopping list: hunt the enemy's anti-air vehicle to cover your weakness to aircraft, or a heavy tank for its cannon. Each target previews what it would give.
The stolen weapon lasts for this life; on death it drops as a contested salvage crate instead of vanishing.
A new claim asks whether to keep the current stolen weapon or swap; a deliberate hold-to-replace reads better than the RTS's locked slot.
as_target: A tether on you is a countdown: if you die now, the enemy gets your gun. Get out of range, break line of sight, or burst the rooted claimer.
Damaged vehicles near a leecher should retreat earlier: 'don't feed' becomes a skill.
Seeing your own weapon on an enemy tank is readable and gives a revenge goal: kill it and the weapon drops as salvage.
teammates: Claim and finish: the leecher pings its tethered target and allies burst it, because the claim doesn't need the killing blow.
Escort the leecher while it is rooted and its gun is quiet.
The team decides which weapon to take, based on what the team lacks.
Friendly donations are limited to wrecks or abandoned allied vehicles, to stop teammates farming each other.
controls: Hold right mouse: tether to the vehicle under the cursor while in range and line of sight.
Q or slot 2: fire the stolen weapon on its own trigger and cooldown (no hidden alternation with the main gun).
Hold E for about a second: discard or replace the stolen weapon when a new claim would overwrite it.
A context ping on the tethered target: 'leeching, finish it'.
feedback: A thick beam in the leecher's team colour that pulses with the drain, and a hum that rises as the target's health drops.
A ring and icon over the target that preview the weapon you would get.
On a claim: a distinct sound, the weapon visibly snapping onto the chassis, and the donor's icon in the HUD slot.
On the target: a red edge vignette and a 'leeched' warning with an arrow to the source.
Each stolen weapon class has an oversized, distinct attachment model readable from above; claimable wrecks glow and show a despawn ring.
changes_from_rts: Map the donor table to units players can actually buy; RA3's naval and epic donors don't exist here.
Replace RA3's random pick between several leechers with a visible rule, such as first to latch.
Forbid leeching your own living teammates, which invites farming; allow only enemies and abandoned or wrecked allies.
Scale stolen weapons to the leecher's tier so a T2 can't carry a T3 gun at full power.
Give the stolen weapon its own trigger instead of RA3's hidden one-weapon-at-a-time alternation.
Full rooting while leeching may be too punishing in a twitch shooter; consider a heavy slow and a turret lock instead.
Decide what happens to a stolen weapon on death and respawn.

team_play.notes: The claim-at-death rule rewards coordination directly: one player claims, others finish. The enemy has to coordinate its retreats and deny wrecks.

notes: A generic upgrade ladder is cheap: one upgrade track per eligible unit and a pickup.
The donor-specific version needs a donor-to-weapon table plus sockets, models and effects for every stolen weapon on every leecher; content grows with donors times leechers.
The claim at the moment of death must be decided by the server; ties and latency create disputes.
A tether weapon needs range and line-of-sight checks, slow or root states, drain and heal ticks, and break rules.
UI: donor previews, target warnings, kill-feed icons and loadout slot states.
Snowballing: the team winning fights collects the most stolen weapons and wins more fights.
Players hunt the best donor instead of playing the objective.
Stealing anti-air or anti-infantry removes the leecher's designed weakness and flattens the counter wheel.
Cheap units carrying top-tier weapons undermine top-tier prices.
Drain, healing and extra damage together can make the leecher very hard to kill.
Players may not see which stolen weapon an enemy carries unless each class has a distinct, oversized silhouette.
A tank firing another faction's weapon effects can make players misjudge it and pick the wrong counter.
With several beams in a brawl it can be unclear who will get the claim.

variants.name: Tether at death
variants.summary: Hold a beam on the target; whoever is tethered when it dies gets the reward, whoever landed the kill.

variants.name: Donor copy
variants.summary: The gained weapon is a scaled-down copy of the donor's own weapon, so the enemy roster becomes a loot table.

variants.name: Upgrade ladder
variants.summary: Every claim moves the unit one step up a fixed ladder, whatever the donor was; extra claims become cash or experience. Easier to read and balance.

variants.name: Wreck crate race
variants.summary: A kill drops a pickup that the first unit to touch claims, before it decays; enemies can grab or destroy it first.
variants.seen_in: Generals salvage, Battlefield kits, Company of Heroes dropped weapons

variants.name: Kit swap
variants.summary: A pickup replaces the whole loadout or class instead of adding a weapon.

variants.name: Loot as currency
variants.summary: Wrecks pay out in resources or crafting material rather than direct power.
variants.seen_in: Supreme Commander reclaim, ARC Raiders salvage

variants.name: Limited-ammo copy
variants.summary: The gained weapon runs on limited energy or ammo and fades when it runs dry.

variants.name: Live extraction
variants.summary: Rip a consumable out of a living target, damaging it, and carry it to yourself or an ally; the carrier drops it on death.

variants.name: Revive the husk
variants.summary: Heavy units leave a fragile wreck that an engineer from either side can bring back for their own team at reduced health.

variants.name: Cannibalize allies
variants.summary: Takes modules from friendly units too, destroying them, trading team strength for one strong unit.

variants.name: Whole-vehicle steal
variants.summary: Takes the vehicle itself rather than a part; the thief climbs out when it is destroyed and can try again.
variants.seen_in: Generals and Tiberian Sun hijackers, Halo boarding

adds_strengths.why: Gains a weapon from kills that can cover its own gaps.

adds_weaknesses.why: Starts each life without its best weapon, and a poor claim can fill the slot.

counters.why: Every vehicle it helps kill can arm it.

countered_by.why: Ground claimers usually can't tether aircraft and have no anti-air until they steal it.
Fast targets leave tether range before they die.
Punishes it while it is busy claiming.

open_questions: What happens to a stolen weapon on death: lost, dropped as salvage, or kept until the round resets?
Should the slot lock once filled (as in RA3), be replaceable, or run on limited ammo?
Should leeching be one faction's signature (the Soviets, in RA3's spirit) or shared by all factions?
In a multi-seat vehicle, who controls the stolen weapon and the tether?

shooter_fit.reason: Turns every kill into a loadout decision and rewards 'soften and claim' team play, but needs firm rules (tier scaling, no farming teammates) to avoid snowballing.
